newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Stock markets face test after Dow falls.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Stock markets face test after Dow falls.

text.p: British blue chips have racked up gains of two percent so far in January -- the month some use as a barometer to forecast the year -- but stock markets face another test as the month comes to a close given Wall Street's recent losing streak, stock strategists said on Wednesday.
The Dow Industrial Average, up by about 100 points at one stage on Tuesday, ended the day with a 4.61 point loss, marking the fifth consecutive session that the average fell.
The FTSE 100 index, in turn, fell 28.1 points to 4,209.03 by midday amid growing fears of a U.S.-induced correction.

"With Wall Street up 100 points yesterday, things were looking quite positive, but then it finished lower. Wall Street is looking a bit tired and there is no enthusiasm for anything today," one trader complained.
Sentiment on Wall Street soured as U.S. bond yields rose on Tuesday.

The wild gyrations in U.S. stocks have put investors on edge across most of Europe. In Paris, the CAC 40 Index was off 18.91 points to 2,463.85, while the Madrid General Index fell 6.98 points to 459.49. The Swiss Market Index eased 13.0 points to 4,169.3, but the German DAX Index recovered initial losses and was up 13.72 points to 3,003.05 by midday.

"Volatility is rising. I look for equities and bonds to remain weak," said Kirit Shaw, a stock strategist with Sanwa International. "If the Dow does have a major correction, the FTSE could go down to 3,750 to 3,800."
Robin Griffiths, chart analyst at HSBC James Capel, calls the Dow's recent performance "the beginning of the end" of the bull market.
"The Dow is looking overbought and we are playing an end game," he told told institutional investors at an HSBC James Capel briefing on Tuesday.
Griffiths predicted the U.S. stock market would peak in mid-February before a final "bear market rally" carries it yet to another peak by August or September.

Meanwhile, minutes from the December 11 UK monetary meeting released on Wednesday revealed that Bank of England Governor Eddie George was pressing Chancellor Kenneth Clarke for a half point increase in interest rates in the next few months.
"The governor was quite aggressive in his stance and that's also making the market nervous," said UK equity strategist Cory Miller of Credit Lyonnais Laing.
Yet Miller said he believes Clarke can resist a rate hike up until the general election, which must be held by May, since the strength of the sterling has served to dampen economic growth.
Relatively low interest and inflation rates, plus good prospects for dividends and share buybacks from British corporations should keep UK stocks buoyant, he added.
Peter Chambers, global strategist with HSBC James Capel, figures the British stock market can weather a slow decline on Wall Street.

"If Wall Street collapsed, we'd obviously come off. But if it does nothing or falls gradually, UK stocks would have scope to continue to rise," said Chambers, whose year end target for the FTSE 100 is 4,350. "(UK shares) are still cheap compared to other markets."
SocGen equity strategist Andy Hartwill, however, said the next hurdle for stocks would not be a setback on Wall Street, but rather disappointing earnings from British companies.
"Further signs of sterling's strength will come back to haunt the market during reporting season. That will be the most likely source of disappointment," said Hartwill.
